## Project overview

> ### Project description:

> - [Title]{.underline}: A Network Meta-Analysis of Interventions for Students Struggling with Mathematics in Grades K-6

> - [Purpose]{.underline}: Identify which multicomponent mathematics interventions are most associated with improved math outcomes amongst struggling students.

> - [Method]{.underline}: The project uses a network meta-analysis to estimate and rank the relative impact of multicomponent mathematics interventions on student-level math outcomes in a single analysis model.

> - [Significance]{.underline}: Provides evidence to stakeholders on the comparative effectiveness of multicomponent mathematics interventions, particularly amongst struggling students.

> ### Goals:

> - **RQ: *Which types of multicomponent mathematics interventions most improve math outcomes amongst grade school students struggling in math?***

> - Conduct network meta-analysis of mathematics interventions targeting students struggling with mathematics to identify which interventions (coded as combinations of instructional practices) are most associated with improved outcomes.

> - Disseminate findings to educators, administrators, and other key decision makers and stakeholders.

> ### Steps:

> 1)  [Systematic review]{.underline}:\
>     Conduct a systematic review of relevant research to identify high-quality, credible research to be included in the meta-analysis synthesis.

> 2)  [Network meta-analysis (NMA):]{.underline}\
>     Fit a network meta-analysis to the student-level outcomes of this research to identify the instructional practice combinations most associated with improved outcomes.

> 3)  [Component network-analysis (CNMA):]{.underline} Fit a component network meta-analysis to the student-level outcomes of this research to identify the individual instructional components most associated with improved outcomes.

> ### Role:

> - Co-led project with [Instructional Research Group](https://www.inresg.org/) & Dean of the College of Education at University of Oregon.

> - Individually lead the development of all R scripts: data cleaning/wrangling, indicator creation, analysis, and visualization of findings.

> - Participated in the systematic review effort for identifying high-quality, credible research findings for inclusion in project.

> - Credentials:
>   - ***Domain knowledge***: Deep K–12 and postsecondary domain knowledge built through long term design, analysis, and review of education studies.
>   - ***Trained in research evaluation standards and statistical methods***: Certified WWC reviewer for over a decade conducting systematic reviews, calculating and synthesizing effect sizes, and producing WWC products such as intervention reports and practice guides.
>   - ***Experienced statistical programmer***: Advanced Stata and R programming for data processing, analysis, and reporting.

## Methodology

> ### Systematic review

> - Identify relevant group‑design studies (studies that compare student-level outcomes for an intervention group against a comparison group) that estimate the effect of a multicomponent mathematics intervention on student-level math outcomes amongst grade schoolers struggling with math.

> - Keep only those studies that meet [What Works Clearinghouse](https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc) evaluation design and analysis standards (i.e., rigorous, high-quality studies).

> - Each finding has been converted to a standardized measure of intervention effects, known as an effect size, so that outcomes measures on different scales can be synthesized on a common scale.

> - Analysis database is therefore comprised of student-level outcomes (as effect sizes) nested within study contrasts and studies. (45 studies; 77 contrasts; 300 unique student-level effect estimates)

> ### Network meta-analysis

> - ***Meta-analysis***
>   - Meta‑analysis is a quantitative synthesis method that combines effect sizes from multiple independent studies to estimate a pooled average effect with greater precision than any single study.
>   - Meta‑analysis compares one intervention against one comparator at a time (e.g., A vs. B). It pools results only from studies that directly evaluate that specific contrast, so each comparison is analyzed in isolation.

> - ***Network meta-analysis (NMA)***
>   - Network meta‑analysis (NMA) extends this by comparing three or more interventions simultaneously within a connected evidence network.
>   - NMA synthesizes in a single analysis both direct evidence (head‑to‑head trials) and indirect evidence.
>   - For example: A vs. C inferred through the connection (network) of A vs. B and B vs. C, allowing estimation of all pairwise effects even when some comparisons have never been tested directly.

> - ***Advantages of NMA***:
>   - <u>Indirect comparisons</u> — NMA estimates effects between interventions lacking head‑to‑head trials (e.g., A vs. C via B).
>   - <u>Simultaneous multi‑arm synthesis</u> — integrates all interventions in one coherent model rather than running many separate analyses.
>   - <u>Intervention ranking</u> — produces hierarchies identifying which interventions are most effective (e.g., model estimates and p-scores).
>   - <u>Greater precision</u> — combining direct & indirect evidence expands the evidence base providing greater analytical precision in estimation.
>   - <u>Efficient use of sparse evidence</u> — leverages all available comparisons, even when direct evidence is limited.

> - ***Challenges with education data***
>   - Dependencies in education meta‑analysis—multiple measures nested within contrasts (study arms) nested within studies—create correlated sampling errors, which biases model estimates if ignored in the analysis
>   - The R package *netmeta* assumes independence and therefore struggles with the multi‑level, multi‑measure data typical in education research
>   - The function ***rma.mv()*** of the *metafor* package can model those dependencies directly, making it better suited for NMA in such contexts.

> ### metafor::rma.mv()

> - [*metafor*](https://wviechtb.github.io/metafor/index.html)- a comprehensive collection of functions for conducting meta-analyses in R (author: Wolfgang Viechtbauer)

> - [**rma.mv()**](https://wviechtb.github.io/metafor/reference/rma.mv.html)- a function to fit meta-analytic multivariate/multilevel fixed- and random/mixed-effects models with or without moderators via linear (mixed-effects) models.

> ### Fitting the NMA ###:

> - Interventions enter the analysis model as contrast-coded moderators (1, 0, -1).

> - Entering contrast‑coded intervention columns as moderators in **rma.mv()** turns the model into a network meta‑analysis because the moderator structure encodes the entire treatment network.

> - The fitted moderator coefficients become the pooled relative effects between interventions—estimated simultaneously using all direct and indirect evidence.

> - Interventions are component‑coded, meaning any interventions that share the same combination of instructional components enter the model under the same moderator. This approach identifies which component combinations are most effective and improves interpretability by reducing the noise created by many nominally different but structurally similar interventions.

``` r
    ### Fit NMA model to outcomes in the Whole Numbers domain   
    res_mod_icW <- rma.mv(effect_size, V_list,                              
                          mods = ~ FF + FF.RS + NL.FF.RS + NL.RS + RS + VF.FF.RS + VF.RS - 1, # BAU is excluded to serve as reference level
                          random = ~ 1 | record_id/es_id,                              
                          rho=0.60,                              
                          data=NMA_data_analysis_subset_grpID_icW)     
```

## Next Steps

> - CNMA: Fit a component network meta-analysis to the student-level outcomes of this research to identify the individual instructional components most associated with improved outcomes.

> - R code on GitHub: [NMA_metafor_allnodes_ic.R](https://github.com/Instructional-Research-Group-IRG/network-meta-analysis/blob/main/cNMA/cNMA_metafor_allnodes_ic.R)

``` r
    ### Fit an additive CNMA model to outcomes in the Whole Numbers domain   
    res_mod_icW_cnma <- rma.mv(effect_size, V_list, 
                            mods = ~ FF + RS + NL + SE + VF - 1, # BAU is excluded to serve as the reference level for the comparisons.
                            random = ~ 1 | record_id/es_id, 
                            rho=0.60, 
                            data=cNMA_data_analysis_subset_grpID_icW)
    summary(res_mod_icW_cnma)      
```
